title: Setting out
hookLine: Nanak leaves home for years of travel on foot, with Mardana beside him

lines: A JOB, A FAMILY, A TOWN.
cards: Guru Nanak had a good job in Sultanpur, a wife, two young sons, and a sister nearby who loved him. Then, some time after the river, he left it all and started walking. Not for a weekend.
For years. On foot, with Mardana and the rebab beside him, sleeping where they were offered a floor and eating what they were given. From here the story changes shape.
It stops being one place and becomes a road.

teach.b: Sikhs call these journeys the udasis.

teach.h: THE MAP IS TRADITION, NOT A LOG.
teach.b: Tradition counts four great ones, sometimes five, spread over many years. One went east, toward Bengal and Assam. One went south, as far as Sri Lanka, tradition says.
One north, into the Himalayas. One west, as far as Mecca and Baghdad. Nobody has a travel log.

The routes come from the janamsakhis, life stories written down generations later, and they don't always agree on the order or the route. So the dates and the map are tradition, and Sikh historians still argue over them.

Udasi comes from a word that can mean detachment, even sadness: someone who has stepped back from the world. In Nanak's time it could describe a renunciate, a wandering holy man who gave up home for good.
Here's the surprise. Nanak walked like a renunciate, but he didn't preach renunciation. He came home between journeys, and his hymns don't ask people to abandon their families.

teach.h: NOT AWAY FROM PEOPLE. OUT TO THEM.
teach.b: He went out to people, not away from them: to pilgrimage towns, Muslim shrines, mountain hermitages and markets, talking with whoever was there, priests, Sufis, yogis, carpenters, thieves.
Stop after stop became a story, a short, sharp scene that Sikh children grow up hearing, and the coming lessons take them one at a time.
Everything he'd said at home, there is no Hindu, there is no Muslim, now goes out on the road, to see if it holds up.

how: Sikhs remember Guru Nanak's udasis through the sakhis, short stories of each stop, told at home, in gurdwaras and in children's classes; many gurdwaras across South Asia stand at places tradition links to his travels.

games.q: you're Nanak. you've got a job, a family, and something you've just understood that you can't keep to yourself. what do you do?
o: stay put and write it down.
walk out, for years, to meet people everywhere.

games.why: he walked for years, with Mardana, but he came home between journeys. he went out to people, not away from them.

practice: If you can, stand and take a slow walk: around the room, down the hall, out the door.
Look the way a traveler looks, as if you'll have to describe it to someone back home: the light, the sounds, one thing you've never noticed before.

wordCard.voice: Udasi. The name for Guru Nanak's long journeys on foot, from a word for detachment, stepping back. Today's word.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: udasi, from a word for detachment or sadness; for Sikhs, the name of Guru Nanak's journeys.

carryVoice: Your line: go and see. Tomorrow, a carpenter's coarse bread in Saidpur. Thirty-two days walked.
